Law and Gospel
LAW and GOS-pul
noun phrase (Reformed and Lutheran theology)
The fundamental theological distinction between the law (which commands and condemns, revealing sin and driving the sinner to Christ) and the gospel (which freely offers salvation in Christ to the believing sinner). Central to both Lutheran and Reformed theology, though with substantive differences in emphasis and application.

📖 Biblical Definition

The fundamental theological distinction between the law and the gospel. The law is God's commandment, which reveals His holy character, prescribes perfect obedience, exposes and condemns sin, and (for the unbeliever) drives him to despair of self-righteousness and (in the Spirit's work) to Christ. The gospel is the good news of salvation freely offered in Christ to the believing sinner — not a new law to be obeyed for salvation but the proclamation of what Christ has accomplished. The distinction is central to both Lutheran and Reformed theology, though with substantive differences. In Lutheran theology, the law-gospel distinction is the principal hermeneutical key: every text is to be rightly divided into law (which always accuses, lex semper accusat) and gospel (which always comforts); the law's principal use is to drive the sinner to Christ; the believer lives by the gospel. In Reformed theology, the law-gospel distinction is affirmed but held within the broader framework of the covenant of grace and the three uses of the law (especially the third use, the law as the rule of grateful obedience for the believer); the Reformed tradition emphasizes more strongly than Lutheran theology the abiding positive role of the law in the believer's sanctification. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive law-gospel distinction (the law commands and condemns; the gospel freely saves; justification is by the gospel through faith, not by the law through works) while holding it within the Reformed framework of the covenant of grace and the three uses of the law, affirming the abiding positive role of the moral law as the rule of the believer's grateful obedience (against the antinomian misuse of the law-gospel distinction to dismiss the law's third use).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The fundamental distinction between the law (which commands and condemns, driving the sinner to Christ) and the gospel (which freely offers salvation in Christ); central to Lutheran and Reformed theology, with the Reformed tradition emphasizing the law's abiding third use in sanctification.

LAW AND GOSPEL, n. phr. (Reformed and Lutheran theology) The distinction between the law (God's commandment, which reveals His character, prescribes perfect obedience, exposes and condemns sin, drives the sinner to Christ) and the gospel (the good news of salvation freely offered in Christ to the believing sinner). Central to both Lutheran and Reformed theology. Lutheran: the principal hermeneutical key; law always accuses (lex semper accusat), gospel always comforts. Reformed: affirmed but held within the covenant of grace and the three uses of the law, emphasizing the law's abiding third use (the rule of grateful obedience). Held against the antinomian misuse that dismisses the law's third use.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 3:19-20 — "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin."

Galatians 3:24 — "Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith."

Romans 10:4 — "For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth."

Psalm 119:97 — "O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The antinomian misuse of the law-gospel distinction dismisses the law's abiding third use (the rule of grateful obedience); the legalist misuse confuses law and gospel, making justification depend on law-keeping.

expand to see more

The law-gospel distinction is held against two opposing misuses. The legalist misuse confuses law and gospel, making justification depend on the sinner's law-keeping; this contradicts the gospel's free offer of salvation in Christ apart from works (Romans 3:20, 28; Galatians 2:16). The antinomian misuse abuses the law-gospel distinction to dismiss the law's abiding positive role in the believer's life; treating the law as wholly negative (only accusing, never guiding), the antinomian denies the third use of the law (the moral law as the rule of the believer's grateful obedience). The Reformed-confessional tradition holds the substantive law-gospel distinction (justification is by the gospel through faith, not by the law through works) while affirming the abiding positive role of the moral law (the third use, the rule of grateful obedience in sanctification). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the Reformed framework: the law commands and condemns the unbeliever, driving him to Christ; the gospel freely saves the believing sinner; the moral law continues as the rule of the justified believer's grateful obedience, written on the heart by the Spirit in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The distinction between law (commands and condemns) and gospel (freely saves); central to Lutheran and Reformed theology; Reformed emphasis on the law's third use; held against antinomianism and legalism.
